text: In the Augustan Roman world, Vitruvius describes the chorobates as a roughly twenty-foot straightedge on legs. Hanging plumb lines had to coincide with marks on its crosspieces before the surveyor treated it as level; this established the fall available for a water channel (Book VIII.5).

text: Vitruvius offers a second reading for the chorobates when wind makes its plumb lines unsteady: water in a groove along the beam should meet both rims evenly. His Roman surveying account uses one instrument with two independent indicators of level (Book VIII.5).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: Vitruvius recommends a city reservoir divided into three distributing compartments: one for public basins and fountains, one for baths, and one for private houses. In his Augustan Roman design, separating supplies protects public water from private diversion (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: In his Roman aqueduct recommendations, Vitruvius specifies a sloping masonry channel covered by a vault to shield the water from direct sun. The conduit is a protected route with a measured descent, rather than simply an open trench (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: Where hills interrupt an aqueduct route, Vitruvius recommends tunnelling at the required gradient. In loose earth or sand he calls for vaulted masonry and access shafts spaced along the route; his first-century BCE account treats ground conditions as a design constraint (Book VIII.6).

text: Vitruvius argues that baked-clay water pipes are preferable to lead pipes, citing both taste and harm associated with lead. This is a recommendation in an Augustan Roman technical text, rather than evidence that every Roman water system avoided lead (Book VIII.6).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: Vitruvius describes a Roman water-lifting drum divided into eight compartments. Workers tread it round so water enters at the rim and exits near the axle into a trough: it moves a large volume but does not lift it very high (Book X.4).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: For a greater lifting height, Vitruvius describes bronze buckets on a double iron chain running around an axle. Each bucket tips its water into a reservoir as it passes over the top, turning intermittent scoops into a continuous supply (Book X.4).
provenance: Original factual paraphrase. Vitruvius, De architectura, Augustan Roman world, translated by Morris Hicky Morgan (1914), public-domain primary text; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/20239/20239-h/20239-h.htm . Chapters specified in the stimulus.

text: Vitruvius describes floatboards attached to a wheel so that a river current turns it and raises water in boxes. In his Augustan Roman account, the current supplies motion that a tread-powered lifting wheel otherwise gets from workers (Book X.5).

text: In Vitruvius’s Roman watermill description, a toothed wheel on the waterwheel axle drives a smaller horizontal toothed wheel attached to the millstone. The paired gears change the direction of rotation while a hopper feeds grain to the stones (Book X.5).

text: Vitruvius explains a steelyard by moving a small counterweight farther along the beam until it balances a larger load. His Roman example makes distance from the pivot as important as the weight itself (Book X.3).

text: Vitruvius recommends northern light for picture galleries because it varies less, and eastern exposure for bedrooms and libraries because their use needs morning light. These are room-by-room prescriptions in an Augustan Roman architectural manual (Book VI.4).
